In order to carry out a PCR experiment using the genomic DNA of a certain animal, it was decided to synthesise artificially an oligonucleotide (a molecule in which a relatively small number of nucleotides are polymerised) to be used as a primer. We want the synthesised oligonucleotide to recognise specifically and hybridise to only one particular site in the genome. For this, it must be designed so that a base sequence completely identical to the synthetic oligonucleotide (the specific base sequence) appears as little as possible at places other than the target site.

At least how many bases long should the synthesised oligonucleotide be so that the expected number of occurrences of the specific base sequence in the whole genome is less than 1? Choose $\underline{\text{the shortest number of bases}}$ from A–L. Assume that the genome size of this animal is 3 billion base pairs and that each base occurs at random in the genome with equal probability. Also, $4^{15} = 1{,}073{,}741{,}824 \approx 10^{9}$. (4 points)

A. 10 bases

B. 11 bases

C. 12 bases

D. 13 bases

E. 14 bases

F. 15 bases

G. 16 bases

H. 17 bases

I. 18 bases

J. 19 bases

K. 20 bases

L. 21 bases

Among the codons of mRNA, the stop codons were not identified in the research of M. Nirenberg and colleagues, who worked on deciphering the genetic code; they were elucidated by experiments using alkaline phosphatase-deficient mutants of Escherichia coli. On circumstantial evidence, it had been thought that in these mutants alkaline phosphatase was no longer made because a particular codon in the alkaline phosphatase gene had changed into a stop codon. When new mutations were induced in these mutants by treatment with an agent that causes single-base substitutions, cells in which alkaline phosphatase activity was restored (revertants) appeared. Alkaline phosphatase protein was isolated from the revertants, its amino acid composition was analysed and compared with that of the wild type; depending on the revertant, the amino acids of the alkaline phosphatase were the same as in the wild type or slightly different. Where they differed, compared with the wild type, there was one tryptophan fewer and instead one more of lysine, glutamine or tyrosine.

B. UAG

C. UGA

D. UAA and UAG

E. UAA and UGA

G. UAA, UAG and UGA

In the traditional process of making sake, steamed rice on which kōji mould (麹菌) has been grown and water are put into an open vat, and the temperature is raised little by little from a low temperature of about 5 °C while the mixture is stirred slowly. The kōji mould dies as soon as the water is added, but the starch of the steamed rice is gradually broken down into sugars by the amylase that the kōji mould has secreted. Because the fermentation vat is deep and its contents are thick and mushy, the oxygen is soon used up even though the system is open. Over about one month various microorganisms succeed one another; in what order will the four kinds of microorganisms shown below become dominant? Choose from A–L the one showing the correct order. (5 points)

① Sake yeast: the only eukaryote; grows slowly. It carries out alcoholic fermentation, in which sugars are broken down to produce ethanol. It is sensitive to alkaline environments but very resistant to acidic environments. It can grow both in environments with oxygen and in anaerobic environments without oxygen.

② Bacillus subtilis (枯草菌): grows fast and forms heat-resistant spores. It is an aerobic bacterium that requires oxygen for growth. It is relatively resistant to alkaline environments but sensitive to acidic environments. It is highly sensitive to chemical substances with antibacterial properties, such as nitrite.

③ Lactic acid bacteria: carry out lactic acid fermentation, in which sugars are broken down to produce lactic acid. When oxygen is present they carry out hardly any lactic acid fermentation. They are sensitive to alcohol.

④ Bacteria of the genus Pseudomonas: aerobic bacteria that require oxygen for growth, but many of them have nitrate-reducing ability and use nitrate as an electron acceptor instead when the oxygen runs out. They prefer a pH near neutral.

Read the following passage on alcohol metabolism in humans, and choose from A–L the appropriate combination of what goes into the brackets ( ). (5 points)

When a human ingests ethanol, it is broken down to acetic acid by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH). Acetaldehyde, the intermediate product of this reaction, is a toxic chemical substance and, when it accumulates in the body, is a cause of hangovers and the like.

$$\text{ethanol} \;\overset{\text{ADH}}{\rightleftharpoons}\; \text{acetaldehyde} \;\overset{\text{ALDH (e.g. ALDH2)}}{\rightleftharpoons}\; \text{acetic acid}$$

Genetic polymorphisms are found in the enzymes involved in this reaction. For one of the ALDH genes (ALDH2) there are the allele Glu$^{504}$, which encodes active ALDH2 whose 504th amino acid is glutamic acid, and the allele Lys$^{504}$, which encodes inactive ALDH2 whose 504th amino acid is lysine. ALDH2 forms one enzyme molecule as a tetramer, and it does not have sufficient activity as an enzyme unless all four subunits making up one molecule are of the active type. For this reason, people who have ( ア ) have a constitution that makes them more prone to hangovers and less tolerant of alcohol.

When the gene frequencies of ALDH2 were examined in a certain human population, 77% were of the Glu$^{504}$ type and 23% of the Lys$^{504}$ type. In this population, which is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the proportion of people who are less tolerant of alcohol because of the ALDH2 polymorphism, that is, by constitution, is thought to be about ( イ )%.

Some plant organs show a bending response to particular stimuli. Such bending responses include tropisms, in which the direction of bending is determined by the direction of the stimulus, and nastic movements (nasties), in which the direction of bending is fixed regardless of the direction of the stimulus. Plant bending responses are classified into various types by combining the way the direction of bending is determined with the kind of stimulus that causes the bending.

Sundews (モウセンゴケ類) are a group of insectivorous plants that have glandular hairs covered with mucilage on the surface of their leaves. When a sundew leaf catches an insect in the mucilage, it bends so as to wrap around the insect and digests it inside. The bulleted list below is an outline of the results of experiments on the bending of this leaf carried out on one species of sundew.

Experimental results

• When a living fruit fly was attached to the upper side of a leaf, the leaf bent towards it within a short time.
• When an intact dead fruit fly was attached to the upper side of a leaf, the leaf eventually bent towards it, but it took a long time before the bending occurred.
• When a crushed dead fruit fly was attached to the upper side of a leaf, the leaf bent towards it within a short time.
• When a small stone about the same size as a fruit fly was attached to the upper side of a leaf, no bending occurred.
• When the upper side of a leaf was rubbed with a brush, no bending occurred.

From these results, what type of response is the bending of the sundew leaf thought to be? Choose from A–H the most appropriate answer. (5 points)

A. It is thought to be thigmotropism.

B. It is thought to be thigmonasty.

C. It is thought to be chemotropism.

D. It is thought to be chemonasty.

E. It is thought to be thigmotropism or thigmonasty, but which of the two cannot be determined from these experimental results.

F. It is thought to be thigmotropism or chemotropism, but which of the two cannot be determined from these experimental results.

G. It is thought to be thigmonasty or chemonasty, but which of the two cannot be determined from these experimental results.

H. It is thought to be chemotropism or chemonasty, but which of the two cannot be determined from these experimental results.

Haemoglobin in human red blood cells binds reversibly to oxygen molecules. Haemoglobin with oxygen bound is called oxyhaemoglobin, and haemoglobin without bound oxygen is called deoxyhaemoglobin. In muscle there is myoglobin, which binds reversibly to oxygen molecules.

The figure shows the oxygen dissociation curves of myoglobin (curve 1) and of haemoglobin under various conditions. The oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin isolated and purified from red blood cells (curve 2) differs from that of haemoglobin in red blood cells (curve 3). This is because 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) present in red blood cells binds to deoxyhaemoglobin and changes its affinity for oxygen. It is also known that when people living on the plains move to high altitude, the concentration of 2,3-BPG changes within a few days and a rapid change occurs in the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin in the red blood cells (curve 4).

In general, fertilisation is a biologically important event in which a sperm that has entered the egg fuses with the egg nucleus and the development of a new individual begins.

In sea urchin eggs, a sperm that has reached the egg surface enters the egg within 1 minute. The sperm that has entered the egg forms a sperm nucleus and moves through the egg cytoplasm, and 30 minutes after insemination (the addition of sperm) it fuses with the egg nucleus. After that, cell division (nuclear division) occurs about once an hour. The motile mechanisms of the actin filament system and of the microtubule system are involved in the process of fertilisation.

Cytochalasin B is an inhibitor that suppresses the motile mechanism of the actin filament system. Colcemid is an inhibitor that suppresses the motile mechanism of the microtubule system. Sea urchin eggs were inseminated in sea water containing each of these inhibitors at different concentrations. In addition, eggs were first inseminated in sea water and transferred 10 minutes later to sea water containing each concentration of the inhibitor. When the fertilisation rate, judged by the rate of nuclear fusion, was plotted on the vertical axis against the concentration of each inhibitor in the sea water on the horizontal axis, the results in Figures 1 and 2 were obtained.

What can be learned from these figures about the functions of the actin filament system and the microtubule system in the process of fertilisation? Choose the most appropriate combination from A–I. (5 points)

To investigate the mechanism of formation of the head skeleton of vertebrates, the following experiments 1–3 were carried out and results were obtained.

Experiment 1: When the endoderm region located at the very front of the head of quail and duck embryos was removed and development was allowed to continue, in neither embryo did the skeleton of the anterior part of the head, including the region of the beak, form.

Experiment 2: Only the neural crest cells of quail and duck embryos were labelled with a fluorescent substance before their migration, so that the neural crest cells could be traced after migration. When the endoderm cells located at the very front of the head were then removed, migration of the neural crest cells to the anterior part of the head was observed, but the skeleton of the anterior part of the head did not form.

Experiment 3: Before the neural crest cells migrated to the anterior part of the head, the neural crest at the site where those neural crest cells were located was exchanged by transplantation between quail and duck embryos, and development was allowed to continue. As a result, in quails into which duck neural crest had been transplanted, the shape of the skeleton of the anterior part of the head, including the beak, was of the duck type, and in ducks into which quail neural crest had been transplanted, the shape of the skeleton of the anterior part of the head, including the beak, was of the quail type.

⑤ The information that promotes the formation of the skeleton is carried by the head endoderm.

⑥ The information that promotes the formation of the skeleton is carried by both the neural crest cells and the head endoderm.

Some animals have the ability to determine their own position. Spalax ehrenbergi is a species of rodent that lives underground like a mole and has lost its ability to see. Because this animal cannot use visual information to determine its position, it is thought to use information other than vision. To test this possibility, the following experiment was carried out.

(1) A maze as in Figure 1 is prepared. Food is placed at the exit. One section is 20 cm long, and the shortest route from the entrance to the exit is 160 cm long.

Nukazuke (糠漬け, rice-bran pickles) is a traditional Japanese fermented food. If the care of the bran bed is neglected, a white film is observed spread thickly over the surface because of the film-forming yeasts. Apomeiosis is a type of apomixis in which meiosis changes into a mitosis-like division, so that diploid female gametes are produced and seeds are formed without fertilisation.

Next, the function of a gene that promotes ( ウ ), which is characteristic of prophase of the first division, is knocked out. In this way the separation of ( ア ) in meiosis I is achieved, and gene exchange between the chromosomes derived from the two parents can be prevented. However, because ( エ ) does not occur after the completion of the first division, if the cell proceeds directly to meiosis II the chromosome number is halved and abnormal chromosome segregation occurs. Therefore a genetic mutation that prevents the second division from occurring is introduced.

Through this series of manipulations, diploid female gametes are formed without going through meiosis. If a mutation that causes ( オ ) of the female gametes can then be introduced, the production of seeds by apomeiosis becomes possible.

From studies of mutants and other work on the floral organs of Arabidopsis thaliana (シロイヌナズナ), the ABC model, which explains the mechanism by which floral organs are determined, has been proposed. In this ABC model, as shown in the figure, the floral meristem is divided, from the outside, into four regions: region 1 (sepals), region 2 (petals), region 3 (stamens) and region 4 (pistil). The floral organ of each region is then determined by the combination of genes acting in that region.

The ABC model consists mainly of three rules.

Rule 1: A-class genes determine the development of sepals; A-class genes and B-class genes, of petals; B-class genes and C-class genes, of stamens; and C-class genes, of the pistil.

Rule 2: A-class genes and C-class genes repress each other's expression.

Rule 3: In addition to their role in determining the development of floral organs, C-class genes also suppress the function of the stem cells present in the floral meristem and promote the switch from indeterminate to determinate growth. Consequently, once the floral organs have been formed, the growth of floral organs stops there.

④ A pistil arises in region 1.

⑤ Development of pistils occurs repeatedly in region 4.

⑥ Development of secondary flowers (floral organs consisting of sepals and petals) occurs repeatedly in region 4.

The horizontal axis is the wavelength of light (nm), and the vertical axis is the absorbance per 1 mmol/L; between 470 nm and 660 nm it is magnified 10 times (central vertical-axis scale), and from 660 nm towards longer wavelengths it is magnified a further 10 times (right vertical-axis scale). Absorbance is defined as follows.

When light passes through a light-absorbing substance, the light is absorbed and its intensity decreases. Using the intensity $I_0$ of the irradiated light of a particular wavelength and the intensity $I$ of the transmitted light, the transmittance $T$ is defined by

$$T = \frac{I}{I_0}$$

In actual measurements, if the transmitted light becomes too weak it cannot be measured accurately, and $T$ needs to be at least about 0.01 (1%). The logarithm of the reciprocal of $T$ is the absorbance $A$:

$$A = \log_{10}\frac{I_0}{I} = -\log_{10}\frac{I}{I_0} = -\log_{10}T$$

For a particular substance, the following relationship holds (the Lambert–Beer law).

$$A = K \times c \times l$$

[where $K$: a constant for each substance and wavelength, $c$: concentration of the substance, $l$: optical path length (the length of the substance through which the light passes)]

Here, $K$ at a concentration of 1 mol/L and an optical path length of 1 cm is called the molar absorption coefficient and is denoted by ε. That is, the vertical axis of the graph shows the absorbance $A$ per 1 mmol/L of concentration and per 1 cm of optical path length. The numbers shown at the peaks of the spectra in the figure are the peak wavelengths.

As shown in the table, all amino acids except methionine (Met) and tryptophan (Trp) have more than one codon. For example, glycine (Gly) corresponds to the 4 codons GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG. Because of this redundancy (degeneracy), even if the third base, C, of the codon GGC changes to A by mutation, the amino acid does not change. Such base substitutions that are not accompanied by a change of amino acid are called synonymous substitutions. On the other hand, if the first base of the same GGC is substituted, the amino acid changes to serine (Ser) for G→A, to arginine (Arg) for G→C and to cysteine (Cys) for G→U; whatever the substitution, the amino acid changes. Such base substitutions that are accompanied by a change of amino acid are called non-synonymous substitutions.

The genetic information of organisms is represented by the sequence of the four kinds of bases contained in DNA [adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T)]. One of the methods for determining a base sequence is the Sanger method.

In the Sanger method, a single strand of the DNA to be analysed is used as the template, and DNA fragments are synthesised in a reaction mixture containing one kind of primer that binds specifically to the template DNA, eight kinds of nucleotides (four kinds of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates and four kinds of dideoxyribonucleoside triphosphates) and DNA polymerase. The dideoxyribonucleoside triphosphates are labelled with fluorescence of a different colour for each of the four bases (A: red, C: yellow, G: green, T: blue), and when one of them is incorporated into the growing new DNA strand, elongation of that strand stops. The synthesised single-stranded DNA is subjected to agarose gel electrophoresis with fluorescence detection, and the base sequence is read from the pattern of the bands obtained.

The mark–recapture method is one of the methods for estimating the number of individuals in a population. The basic procedure of this method is as follows. $m$ individuals are captured at random from the population, marked and returned to the original population (first capture). After a certain period, $c$ individuals are captured at random from the population, and $r$ of them are found to be marked (second capture). The number of individuals in the population ($N$) is estimated from the relation $N : m = c : r$ as

$$N = \frac{mc}{r} \qquad (1)$$

Here s is a value called the selection coefficient; in general it indicates by how much the relative fitness of the other genotypes is lower than that of the genotype with the highest fitness. Semi-dominance (半顕性, also called 半優性) is the state in which neither allele is dominant or recessive and the effects of the two alleles are equal.
